name: Teachers-union public choice: from Friedman 1955 to Sowell's Charter Schools and Their Enemies
scope: The applied-public-choice ladder for K-12 education. T1: MILTON FRIEDMAN'S 1955 essay 'THE ROLE OF GOVERNMENT IN EDUCATION' (in Robert Solo, ed., Economics and the Public Interest, Rutgers UP 1955) argued that even if the STATE should FUND schooling, it does not follow that the state must PRODUCE it -- fund the pupil (via vouchers), not the building. The essay is the founding text of the school-choice movement. T2: the empirical anchor case: the DC OPPORTUNITY SCHOLARSHIP PROGRAM, enacted 2004 as part of the DC School Choice Incentive Act. Congress funded scholarships (~$8,000-$12,000) for low-income DC families to attend private schools. Multi-year IES / Wolf-Kisida evaluations (US Dept of Education 2010, 2018) found statistically-significant graduation-rate gains for scholarship recipients. Congressional attempts to shut it down came repeatedly from the same district's teachers-union allies. T3: the CHICAGO TEACHERS UNION strike sequence -- 2012 (9 school days), 2019 (11 days), 2022 (5 days) -- each closing schools for ~300,000 K-12 children. The advocate's SEEN pitch is 'fair pay and smaller classes'; the UNSEEN cost is the ~300,000 children who are not learning, disproportionately low-income, whose parents cannot easily choose an alternative. T4: THOMAS SOWELL, 'CHARTER SCHOOLS AND THEIR ENEMIES' (Basic Books 2020) -- Sowell's late-career book comparing NYC charter-school and district-school test scores for demographically-matched cohorts in the SAME BUILDINGS (charters and district schools that literally share a physical structure under NYC 'co-location' rules). Sowell finds charter students outperform in every matched-building comparison; the political opposition to charters, he argues, is a public-choice story about a producer-interest (teachers unions) resisting a competitor. T5: the PATTERN the ladder teaches -- OLSON concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs applied to K-12: the TEACHERS UNION is the concentrated beneficiary that organizes, negotiates, endorses, and staffs school-board elections; the PARENTS AND CHILDREN are the dispersed victim class that pays higher taxes and receives worse outcomes but does not organize. The public-choice question is not 'are teachers bad?' -- it is 'which organized interest is best positioned to shape the rules?' Further rungs: the 1993-95 California Proposition 174 voucher initiative funding fight, in which the California Teachers Association outspent the pro-voucher side roughly 10-to-1 (CORROBORATE AT BUILD); Terry Moe's 'Special Interest: Teachers Unions and America's Public Schools' (Brookings 2011) as the standard academic analysis.

CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'School voucher', 'DC Opportunity Scholarship Program', 'Chicago Teachers Union', 'Charter schools in New York City', 'Milton Friedman' (2026-09-05) -- 1955 essay origin, DC OSP 2004 enactment, Chicago strike dates 2012/2019/2022, Sowell 2020 book, co-location matched-building comparison method. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact IES / Wolf-Kisida DC OSP evaluation graduation-rate figures; exact CTA-vs-voucher California 1993 spending ratio; the exact NYC co-location matched-building sample size in Sowell 2020.

Dinner-test payoff: T4 (Sowell physically comparing charter and district children in the SAME BUILDING and finding one group learns more) and T5 (the pattern is Olson: teachers organize, parents do not). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on Friedman writing in 1955, not 'define school choice.' name: Right-to-try and the FDA: from Peltzman to Vinay Prasad and Alex Tabarrok
scope: The FDA drug-approval ladder that pushes past the classical Peltzman result into the modern right-to-try + accelerated-approval debate. T1: SAM PELTZMAN'S 1973 paper 'AN EVALUATION OF CONSUMER PROTECTION LEGISLATION: THE 1962 DRUG AMENDMENTS' (Journal of Political Economy vol 81) studied the KEFAUVER-HARRIS AMENDMENTS of 1962, passed in response to the THALIDOMIDE tragedy, which imposed proof-of-efficacy requirements on new drug approvals. Peltzman estimated the amendments reduced the flow of new drugs by roughly half and that lives lost from DELAYED approval of effective drugs significantly exceeded lives saved from blocking ineffective ones. T2: the SEEN effect Congress advertised in 1962: thalidomide-style birth defects prevented. The UNSEEN cost Peltzman named: patients dying while safe-and-effective drugs sat in a longer approval queue. T3: ALEX TABARROK (George Mason) has updated the argument for the modern era, chairing the RIGHT-TO-TRY movement that succeeded in the federal RIGHT-TO-TRY ACT (May 2018), which allows terminally-ill patients access to drugs that have passed Phase I safety trials but not yet full FDA approval. The core reasoning move: for a patient with a fatal diagnosis and no approved options, the DEFAULT of 'wait for the FDA' is not safety -- it is death. T4: VINAY PRASAD (UCSF hematologist-oncologist, formerly OHSU) has become the loudest modern critic from a somewhat different angle -- Prasad's 'MALIGNANT: HOW BAD POLICY AND BAD EVIDENCE HARM PEOPLE WITH CANCER' (Johns Hopkins UP 2020) argues that FDA ACCELERATED APPROVAL (a pathway allowing drugs to reach market on surrogate-endpoint evidence like tumor shrinkage rather than survival) has produced many drugs approved on evidence that never converts to actual survival benefit. Prasad's move is not 'less regulation' -- it is 'regulation that judges DRUGS BY RESULTS NOT INTENTIONS.' T5: the SYNTHESIS the ladder teaches: FDA policy sits inside a two-sided error problem. TYPE I errors (approving an unsafe drug) are highly VISIBLE -- thalidomide, Vioxx (Merck withdrawn 2004). TYPE II errors (blocking an effective drug) are highly INVISIBLE -- the patient who died in 1969 while beta-blockers were approved in Europe but not the US does not appear in any headline. Peltzman, Tabarrok, and Prasad all press the same underlying MOVE from different sides: the honest cost-benefit accounts for BOTH error types, not just the seen one. Further rungs: the 21st Century Cures Act (December 2016) as bipartisan reform expanding accelerated pathways; Scott Gottlieb's 2017-19 FDA commissionership as an attempt to speed approvals institutionally; the COVID-19 vaccine EUA process (December 2020) as accelerated approval on the highest-stakes scale in the FDA's history.
source: PRIMARY: Sam Peltzman, 'An Evaluation of Consumer Protection Legislation: The 1962 Drug Amendments' Journal of Political Economy 81 no 5 (Sept 1973); Vinay Prasad, 'Malignant: How Bad Policy and Bad Evidence Harm People with Cancer' (Johns Hopkins UP 2020); Alex Tabarrok, 'Assessing the FDA via the Anomaly of Off-Label Drug Prescribing' Independent Review vol 5 no 1 (Summer 2000). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Kefauver Harris Amendment', 'Right to Try Act', 'Accelerated approval', 'Vinay Prasad', 'Alex Tabarrok' (2026-09-05) -- 1962 amendments post-Thalidomide, Peltzman 1973 study, federal Right-to-Try Act May 2018, Prasad's Malignant 2020, accelerated approval surrogate-endpoint pathway. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact Peltzman 1973 lives-lost estimate wording; exact Right-to-Try Act signing date (widely cited May 30 2018); exact Prasad book publisher and year.
framing_note: The FDA ladder that goes BEYOND the p2 Peltzman entry into the modern right-to-try + accelerated-approval fight. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (Type I errors like thalidomide are visible on every front page; Type II errors -- the patient who died waiting -- never make a headline) and T4 (Prasad's move is not 'less FDA' -- it is 'judge drugs by results not intentions,' the same Friedman move applied to cancer trials). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on Peltzman writing in 1973, not 'define FDA.' BASTIAT PATTERN check: T2 hits SEEN vs UNSEEN directly; T4 is the Friedman results-not-intentions move; T5 is the synthesis of both error types. RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT (LOAD-BEARING): the answer names the reasoning MOVE (Type II error recognition, Friedman results-not-intentions, right-to-try default reversal) or the NAMED CRITIC (Peltzman, Tabarrok, Prasad), NEVER 'the FDA is bad' or 'accelerated approval is good.' Prasad's critique in particular comes from a licensed oncologist inside the medical establishment -- present it that way. DISTRACTOR MINE: other named public-choice moves applied to health (medical licensing per Friedman, Certificate of Need per Sowell), other FDA critics (Henry Miller of Hoover, Robert Higgs), other high-profile drug approvals + withdrawals (Vioxx 2004, beta-blockers). name: The SO2 Acid Rain Program 1990: Coasean tradable permits in practice
scope: The Coase-Theorem-in-practice ladder for environmental policy. T1: RONALD COASE'S 1960 paper 'THE PROBLEM OF SOCIAL COST' (Journal of Law and Economics) argued that when property rights are clearly assigned and transaction costs are low, private bargaining can internalize externalities better than direct command-and-control regulation. The point was not that the initial rights-assignment does not matter -- it was that the STRUCTURE OF THE SOLUTION is bargaining over defined rights, not bureaucratic dictation of technology. T2: the 1990 CLEAN AIR ACT AMENDMENTS, signed by George H.W. Bush on November 15 1990, took the Coasean idea and built the ACID RAIN PROGRAM -- a cap-and-trade market in SULFUR DIOXIDE (SO2) EMISSIONS from coal-fired power plants. Utilities were issued a fixed number of tradable ALLOWANCES; a utility that cut emissions cheaply could SELL its unused allowances; a utility that could not cut cheaply could BUY them. T3: the program worked -- and worked cheaper than command-and-control had predicted. By 2005 US SO2 emissions from power plants had fallen roughly 40% below their 1990 baseline (EPA figures); the compliance cost came in at ~$1B/year against pre-program Congressional-Budget-Office estimates of $4-6B/year (Ellerman, Joskow et al, 'Markets for Clean Air' Cambridge UP 2000). The market did the job at 1/4 to 1/6 the estimated command-and-control cost. T4: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: environmental policy is NOT a choice between 'regulation' and 'unregulated pollution.' It is a choice between COMMAND-AND-CONTROL (a regulator dictates technology and standard) and PROPERTY-RIGHTS + TRADING (a regulator sets the cap and creates a market in the right to emit). Coase's insight was that the SECOND design uses the DISPERSED KNOWLEDGE utilities have about their own abatement costs -- knowledge no regulator can gather -- to route the reductions to whoever can achieve them cheapest. T5: the CONTRAST cases that came after -- the EUROPEAN UNION EMISSIONS TRADING SYSTEM (EU ETS, launched January 2005, the world's largest carbon market, covering ~10,000 installations); the CALIFORNIA CAP-AND-TRADE PROGRAM under AB 32 (launched January 2013, covering ~85% of state emissions); the failed WAXMAN-MARKEY federal cap-and-trade bill (passed House 2009, died in Senate 2010). Each carries the same Coasean logic; each is politically vulnerable to allocation-of-permits capture -- who gets the free initial allowances is a rent-seeking prize (Tullock 1967 applied). Further rungs: the 1968 GARRETT HARDIN 'Tragedy of the Commons' paper (Science) as the pre-Coasean framing that Coase and later Elinor Ostrom both improved on; the acid-rain program itself was proposed within the Bush Sr administration by ECONOMISTS INCLUDING PROJECT 88 (led by Senators Timothy Wirth and John Heinz, drafted by Harvard's Robert Stavins).
source: PRIMARY: Ronald Coase, 'The Problem of Social Cost' Journal of Law and Economics vol 3 (Oct 1960); A. Denny Ellerman, Paul Joskow, Richard Schmalensee, Juan-Pablo Montero, Elizabeth Bailey, 'Markets for Clean Air: The US Acid Rain Program' (Cambridge UP 2000); Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 Title IV. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Acid Rain Program', 'Clean Air Act', 'Emissions trading', 'European Union Emissions Trading System', 'Ronald Coase', 'Coase theorem' (2026-09-05) -- November 15 1990 CAAA signing, tradable SO2 allowances, 40% reduction by 2005, ~$1B/yr realized cost vs $4-6B CBO estimate, EU ETS January 2005 launch, California cap-and-trade AB 32 January 2013 launch, Waxman-Markey 2009 House passage / 2010 Senate death. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact SO2 reduction percentage and year; exact realized vs estimated compliance-cost figures; exact number of installations in EU ETS.
framing_note: The Coase-in-practice ladder -- kids see a REAL market in the RIGHT TO POLLUTE that outperformed the command-and-control alternative. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (a MARKET in the right to emit sulfur dioxide, created by George H.W. Bush's Clean Air Act) and T3 (the market did the job at 1/4 to 1/6 the cost the government's own budget office had estimated). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on Coase writing in 1960, not 'define externality.' BASTIAT PATTERN check: T4 hits KNOWLEDGE-PROBLEM recognition (utilities know their own abatement costs; the regulator does not); T5 hits INCENTIVE RECOGNITION on the permit-allocation capture problem. RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT (LOAD-BEARING): the answer names the reasoning MOVE (Coasean property-rights + trading, knowledge-problem in abatement cost, Tullock rent-seeking in permit allocation) or the NAMED PROGRAM, NEVER 'cap-and-trade is good' or 'command-and-control is bad.' ACCURACY RAIL: Coase himself was skeptical that the 'Coase Theorem' as taught in textbooks was his actual point; the ladder should present the reasoning move as 'property rights + trading over dispersed knowledge,' not as an unconditional endorsement of any specific carbon market. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: if the stem describes the 40% SO2 reduction at 1/4 the projected cost, the answer is not 'markets work' (restatement) -- it is the NAMED PROGRAM (Acid Rain Program 1990), the NAMED ECONOMIST (Coase 1960), or the NAMED REASONING MOVE (dispersed abatement-cost knowledge). DISTRACTOR MINE: other named reasoning moves (Ostrom polycentric commons governance, Pigou-tax framing, Hardin tragedy-of-the-commons), other named environmental programs (Superfund, Endangered Species Act, EU ETS, California AB 32), other 1990 legislation (Americans with Disabilities Act, Immigration Act). CHOICE PARITY: if the answer is a NAMED PROGRAM, all four are environmental programs.
history_overlap: SCIENCE owns the chemistry of sulfur dioxide and acid rain; economics owns the market DESIGN and its cost-effectiveness. GEOGRAPHY owns European vs American vs Californian jurisdictions as places; here they are policy laboratories.

name: The Endangered Species Act perverse incentive: shoot, shovel, and shut up
scope: The classic INCENTIVE-RECOGNITION ladder for conservation policy. T1: the US ENDANGERED SPECIES ACT of 1973, signed by Richard Nixon on December 28 1973, prohibits any 'take' (kill, harm, harass) of a listed species and imposes strict use-restrictions on land designated as critical habitat -- WITHOUT COMPENSATION to landowners whose property values collapse when a listed species is found. T2: the SEEN goal Congress advertised: protect endangered species by protecting their habitat. The UNSEEN incentive the statute created for a landowner: once a listed species is DISCOVERED on your land, your ability to build, farm, log, or develop is drastically constrained, with no payment. The rational landowner response, therefore, is to make sure the species is NEVER DISCOVERED on your land -- by destroying suitable habitat BEFORE the species arrives. T3: the folk name for this pattern among rural landowners is 'SHOOT, SHOVEL, AND SHUT UP' -- shoot the animal if found, bury it, tell nobody. Economist DEAN LUECK and lawyer JEFFREY MICHAEL published 'PREEMPTIVE HABITAT DESTRUCTION UNDER THE ENDANGERED SPECIES ACT' (Journal of Law and Economics 2003) documenting the pattern for the RED-COCKADED WOODPECKER in North Carolina pine forests. They found that landowners near existing woodpecker colonies HARVESTED THEIR PINE TIMBER YOUNGER AND MORE AGGRESSIVELY as the risk of ESA designation rose -- destroying the mature pines the birds needed BEFORE the birds arrived. T4: the REASONING MOVE this reveals: the ESA is a CONCENTRATED COST (borne by whichever specific landowner draws the unlucky draw of a listed species) with a DISPERSED BENEFIT (species preservation shared by everyone). Concentrated-cost / dispersed-benefit is the MIRROR of Olson's more famous concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost pattern; both produce a political-economy failure, but this one produces a BIOLOGICAL failure as well -- the statute causes habitat destruction it was designed to prevent. T5: the reform proposals that follow the diagnosis. JONATHAN ADLER (Case Western Reserve law) has argued in 'Money or Nothing: The Adverse Environmental Consequences of Uncompensated Land-Use Controls' (Boston College Law Review 2008) for shifting to a COMPENSATION model -- pay landowners for the conservation easement rather than confiscate the use rights. Australia's more property-rights-friendly conservation programs (e.g., the Bush Heritage Trust) provide a working contrast. Elinor OSTROM'S polycentric approach applies here too -- local landowner cooperatives with genuine ownership of the conservation problem outperform the top-down federal listing regime. Further rungs: HFPA critical-habitat designations, the KANGAROO RAT case at Stephens' Kangaroo Rat Habitat Conservation Plan in Riverside County CA (1990s), the PACIFIC NORTHWEST spotted-owl fight (1990s) as a related timber-vs-habitat case.
source: PRIMARY: Dean Lueck and Jeffrey Michael, 'Preemptive Habitat Destruction under the Endangered Species Act' Journal of Law and Economics 46 no 1 (April 2003); Jonathan H. Adler, 'Money or Nothing: The Adverse Environmental Consequences of Uncompensated Land-Use Controls' Boston College Law Review 49 no 2 (2008); Endangered Species Act of 1973 (16 USC 1531 et seq). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Endangered Species Act', 'Red-cockaded woodpecker', 'Shoot shovel and shut up', 'Habitat conservation plan' (2026-09-05) -- December 28 1973 Nixon signing, take-prohibition without landowner compensation, Lueck-Michael 2003 red-cockaded woodpecker study, Adler compensation critique. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact Lueck-Michael study finding wording; exact Adler article citation; whether the 'shoot shovel shut up' phrase is documented in a specific interview/testimony or is folk usage.
framing_note: The classic UNINTENDED-CONSEQUENCE ladder for a widely-loved statute. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (landowners near woodpecker colonies harvesting their pines YOUNGER to prevent the birds arriving -- the exact opposite of what the ESA intended) and T4 (a concentrated cost with a dispersed benefit produces preemptive destruction; the statute causes the harm it was designed to prevent). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on Nixon signing the ESA on a specific date, not 'define endangered species.' BASTIAT PATTERN check: T2 hits SEEN (habitat protected) vs UNSEEN (habitat preemptively destroyed); T4 is INCENTIVE RECOGNITION on the mirror of Olson. RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT (LOAD-BEARING): the answer names the reasoning MOVE (concentrated cost + dispersed benefit, preemptive destruction incentive, compensation-vs-confiscation) or the NAMED STUDY (Lueck-Michael 2003), NEVER 'the ESA is bad' or 'species should not be protected.' The ladder is neutral on the SPECIES-PROTECTION GOAL; it critiques the design mechanism. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: if the stem describes the landowner harvesting pines young to prevent the birds arriving, the answer is not 'the ESA has unintended consequences' (restatement) -- it is the NAMED PATTERN ('shoot shovel and shut up' / preemptive habitat destruction), the NAMED STUDY (Lueck-Michael 2003), or the NAMED REASONING MOVE (concentrated cost / dispersed benefit). DISTRACTOR MINE: other named perverse-incentive cases (the Cobra Effect Delhi, Mexico City drivers-buying-second-cars around plate-day restrictions, ethanol mandate destroying feedstocks), other named environmental statutes (Clean Water Act 1972, NEPA 1970, CERCLA/Superfund 1980), other named reasoning moves. name: Agency budget-maximization: TSA, IRS, and the Niskanen pattern in three departments
scope: The Niskanen bureaucrat-budget-maximization move applied across three modern federal agencies. T1: WILLIAM NISKANEN'S 'BUREAUCRACY AND REPRESENTATIVE GOVERNMENT' (Aldine-Atherton 1971) modeled bureaucrats as agents who maximize their AGENCY'S BUDGET (which correlates with their salary, prestige, staff, and career prospects), not agency output as such. The prediction: agencies systematically OVERPRODUCE their nominal service and grow beyond the size that would maximize public welfare. T2: the TRANSPORTATION SECURITY ADMINISTRATION (TSA), created in the Aviation and Transportation Security Act of November 19 2001 in the aftermath of 9/11. Founding staff ~30,000; by 2023 the TSA employed approximately 60,000 (annual budget ~$10B). The measurable output -- prohibited items intercepted, threats prevented -- is difficult to verify, and repeated undercover REDTEAM audits by DHS Inspector General (2015 test found ~95% of contraband was missed; 2017 follow-up finding not much better) suggest the growth is not matched by proportional security gains. T3: the INTERNAL REVENUE SERVICE, whose FY2022 INFLATION REDUCTION ACT (signed August 16 2022 by Joe Biden) provided an additional $80B over ten years and authorized the hiring of an additional ~87,000 IRS employees over a decade. The stated purpose: enforce compliance among high-income taxpayers. The Niskanen prediction: an agency will use expanded budget to grow its own capabilities across the board, not narrowly on the stated target. The 2023-24 audit-rate data will be the empirical test (CORROBORATE AT BUILD). T4: the US DEPARTMENT OF EDUCATION, created by the Department of Education Organization Act (signed October 17 1979 by Jimmy Carter), split off from the old HEW. Its FY2024 budget is approximately $80B; its staff is approximately 4,400. Measured US student outcomes -- NAEP 12th-grade reading and math scores -- have been effectively FLAT from 1979 to 2019 (NAEP long-term trend data). The department has grown; the measurable output on the score it was created to improve has not. T5: the PATTERN Niskanen predicted, VISIBLE in all three cases: growth in staff, budget, and rule-making authority; difficulty in demonstrating proportional improvement in stated OUTPUT; institutional resistance to any measurement scheme that would allow honest comparison of MARGINAL COST vs MARGINAL PRODUCT. The reasoning move: whenever an advocate says 'the agency needs more resources to do its job,' the public-choice critic asks WHAT EVIDENCE is offered that the last 10% of the previous budget produced anywhere near a proportional 10% of the output. Further rungs: JAMES Q. WILSON'S 'BUREAUCRACY: WHAT GOVERNMENT AGENCIES DO AND WHY THEY DO IT' (Basic Books 1989) as the standard non-Austrian account that Niskanen's framework helps interpret; the DOGE ('Department of Government Efficiency') proposal December 2024- as a modern institutional attempt to apply Niskanen's diagnosis.

name: Regulatory capture at the SEC: Harry Markopolos and the Madoff warnings
scope: The dramatic applied-Stigler ladder that shows regulatory capture through what a regulator DID NOT DO. T1: BERNARD MADOFF ran the largest financial fraud in US history -- a $65 BILLION nominal-value Ponzi scheme through his investment-advisory business, unravelled when he confessed to his sons on DECEMBER 10 2008 during the financial crisis. He was arrested the next day and sentenced in June 2009 to 150 years. T2: HARRY MARKOPOLOS, a quantitative analyst working for a Madoff competitor (Rampart Investment Management), figured out by MAY 2000 that Madoff's reported returns were mathematically impossible -- Madoff claimed steady ~1% monthly gains regardless of market conditions, with volatility and Sharpe ratios inconsistent with any real trading strategy. Markopolos filed his FIRST formal SEC complaint in May 2000. T3: Markopolos filed AT LEAST FIVE additional detailed complaints to the SEC -- most notably the NOVEMBER 7 2005 submission titled 'THE WORLD'S LARGEST HEDGE FUND IS A FRAUD,' running 19 pages, containing 29 red flags and mathematical proofs. He testified after Madoff's arrest that he had also warned the WALL STREET JOURNAL and other authorities. The SEC opened investigations but never uncovered the fraud, closing each inquiry without action. T4: the SEC INSPECTOR GENERAL'S POST-MORTEM REPORT ('Investigation of Failure of the SEC to Uncover Bernard Madoff's Ponzi Scheme,' OIG Report 509, August 31 2009) found the SEC had received 'six substantive complaints raising significant red flags' about Madoff between 1992 and 2008 and had failed to investigate any of them adequately -- assigning junior staff, missing basic verification steps (a call to DTCC would have revealed Madoff was not actually trading the volumes he claimed), and failing to understand the trading strategies Madoff described. Markopolos's own book, 'NO ONE WOULD LISTEN' (Wiley 2010), documents the whole sequence from his side. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: GEORGE STIGLER'S 1971 THEORY OF ECONOMIC REGULATION predicted that regulators tend to be captured by the industries they regulate -- to identify with them, defer to them, hire from and to them. The SEC-Madoff failure is not primarily a story of incompetence or corruption -- it is a story of an agency whose STAFF INCENTIVES (career advancement, avoiding embarrassing high-profile investigations of establishment figures, revolving-door prospects) did not align with detecting fraud at a former NASDAQ chairman's firm. name: The FAA and Boeing: 737 MAX certification as regulatory capture
scope: The recent, high-stakes applied-capture ladder from aviation. T1: the BOEING 737 MAX entered commercial service in May 2017 as the fourth-generation update to the 737 line. To match the fuel efficiency of the Airbus A320neo, Boeing mounted larger LEAP-1B engines further forward on the wing, changing the aircraft's pitch behavior at high angles of attack. To hide this handling change from pilots (so airlines could avoid expensive simulator retraining), Boeing added a software system called MCAS -- MANEUVERING CHARACTERISTICS AUGMENTATION SYSTEM -- to push the nose down automatically when a single angle-of-attack sensor read high. T2: two crashes followed. LION AIR FLIGHT 610 (October 29 2018 off Indonesia, 189 dead) and ETHIOPIAN AIRLINES FLIGHT 302 (March 10 2019, 157 dead) both involved MCAS activation from erroneous angle-of-attack readings, with pilots unable to recover the nose-down trim. Total deaths 346. The 737 MAX fleet was grounded worldwide from March 13 2019 to November 18 2020. T3: the CERTIFICATION QUESTION the crashes exposed: HOW had this system been certified? The FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION had, over the previous two decades, progressively DELEGATED much of its certification authority to MANUFACTURER EMPLOYEES themselves via the ORGANIZATION DESIGNATION AUTHORIZATION (ODA) program -- Boeing engineers, working for Boeing, were the ones actually signing off on Boeing designs on behalf of the FAA. The critical MCAS-single-sensor decision, and the removal of MCAS discussion from the pilot's flight manual, were made under this delegated authority without independent FAA review. T4: the OFFICIAL REPORTS. The HOUSE COMMITTEE ON TRANSPORTATION AND INFRASTRUCTURE'S 'FINAL COMMITTEE REPORT: THE DESIGN, DEVELOPMENT, AND CERTIFICATION OF THE BOEING 737 MAX' (September 2020) documented what it called a 'grossly insufficient' certification process and 'a culture of concealment' at Boeing. The DOT INSPECTOR GENERAL'S February 2020 report found the FAA had 'not effectively overseen Boeing's ODA program.' In January 2021 Boeing entered into a $2.5B DEFERRED PROSECUTION AGREEMENT with the DOJ for fraud on the FAA. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: STIGLER'S THEORY OF ECONOMIC REGULATION (1971) predicted that regulated industries capture their regulators. Aviation certification is the STRUCTURAL LIMIT CASE -- the FAA regulates aircraft manufactured by ~two US companies (Boeing and, for regionals, Cessna/Textron); the technical expertise required to certify a modern airliner resides overwhelmingly INSIDE Boeing; and the ODA delegation formalized the capture by making Boeing engineers the de-facto certifiers. The tragedy was not an accident of individual bad actors -- it was an institutional-incentive failure exactly of the type Stigler had described in 1971. Further rungs: the ALASKA AIRLINES FLIGHT 1282 door-plug blowout January 5 2024 as evidence the underlying safety-culture problem persists; the FAA's post-crash reforms including the AIRCRAFT CERTIFICATION SAFETY AND ACCOUNTABILITY ACT (Dec 2020) as institutional response.

name: The lobbying industry: $1.4B (1998) to $4.1B (2023)
scope: The rent-seeking growth ladder that measures Tullock in current dollars. T1: GORDON TULLOCK'S 1967 PAPER 'THE WELFARE COSTS OF TARIFFS, MONOPOLIES, AND THEFT' (Western Economic Journal) introduced the concept of RENT-SEEKING (the term itself was coined later by Anne Krueger 1974): resources devoted to CAPTURING privileges from the state -- lobbying, campaign donations, litigation for regulatory advantage -- are pure DEADWEIGHT LOSS. name: Term-limit resistance: why incumbents oppose the rules that would remove them
scope: Applied constitutional-political-economy ladder for legislative term limits. T1: 15 US STATES have constitutional or statutory TERM LIMITS on their state legislators (California, Colorado, Michigan, Ohio and others -- enacted mostly in the 1990-1994 wave); the US CONGRESS has none. Presidential term limits (two terms max) were added via the TWENTY-SECOND AMENDMENT (ratified February 27 1951 in response to FDR's four terms). Attempts to impose CONGRESSIONAL term limits through state action were struck down in U.S. TERM LIMITS INC v THORNTON (Supreme Court 5-4 decision May 22 1995), which held that only a constitutional amendment can add qualifications for Congress. T2: the CONSTITUTIONAL amendment for congressional term limits polls at 75-83% public support consistently across decades (Gallup, Pew, others); it has never come near the two-thirds House and Senate majorities required to send it to the states, because HOUSE AND SENATE MEMBERS THEMSELVES would have to vote to shorten their own careers. T3: the JAMES BUCHANAN + GORDON TULLOCK 1962 CONSTITUTIONAL POLITICAL ECONOMY frame explains why. AT THE CONSTITUTIONAL LEVEL (rules of the game, chosen behind a veil of uncertainty about your own future position), a rational voter has no idea whether he will be an incumbent or a challenger; he chooses rules that constrain incumbent advantage. AT THE POST-CONSTITUTIONAL LEVEL (choices made within the rules by ACTUAL SITTING INCUMBENTS with known interests), the same person has every incentive to preserve his current advantage. Term limits are the paradigmatic case of a rule the polity clearly wants but the sitting rule-writers cannot rationally choose. T4: the EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE from states. Studies including EINER ELHAUGE ('Are Term Limits Undemocratic?' University of Chicago Law Review 1997) and John Mark Hansen's work on California pre- and post-Proposition 140 (1990) found term limits reduced the incumbency advantage substantially, increased legislative turnover, weakened the seniority-based committee-power structure, and shifted power toward the executive branch, lobbyists, and permanent legislative staff (the actors WHOSE knowledge was NOT term-limited). The reform's effects were REAL but not uniformly what proponents predicted -- a lesson in unintended consequences the Virginia school also predicted. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: WHENEVER a proposed reform requires the CURRENT INCUMBENTS to accept a cost to themselves for a benefit that flows to future citizens or challengers, the DEFAULT EXPECTATION should be that the reform fails to pass, regardless of majority public support. This is not cynicism -- it is Buchanan's constitutional-political-economy analysis of WHICH RULES survive democratic selection at the post-constitutional stage. The same logic explains why GERRYMANDERING REFORM, CAMPAIGN-FINANCE REFORM, and REDISTRICTING REFORM struggle even when broadly popular: those who would lose from the reform are the ones whose votes would enact it. Further rungs: the 1990 California Proposition 140 as the first US legislative term-limits initiative; the ALAN GRAYSON quip 'Congress has term limits: they're called elections' as the incumbent's standard rhetorical parry; SWITZERLAND'S FEDERAL COUNCIL rotating presidency as a live example of a constitutional-level anti-consolidation rule.

name: Political business cycles: Nordhaus 1975, Burns-Nixon 1972, Greenspan-Bush 2004
scope: The Fed-and-the-election-calendar applied-public-choice ladder. T1: WILLIAM NORDHAUS'S 1975 PAPER 'THE POLITICAL BUSINESS CYCLE' (Review of Economic Studies vol 42) formalized the intuition that a monetary or fiscal authority under political pressure will TIME EXPANSIONARY POLICY to precede elections -- producing pre-election boom, post-election bust cycles. The model treats politicians as strategic actors optimizing REELECTION rather than long-run welfare. T2: the ARTHUR BURNS -- RICHARD NIXON case, 1971-72. Burns chaired the Federal Reserve from February 1970 through January 1978. The BURNS WHITE HOUSE TAPES (partially transcribed in Burton Abrams, 'How Richard Nixon Pressured Arthur Burns,' Journal of Economic Perspectives vol 20 no 4, Fall 2006) document Nixon personally pressuring Burns for easier money ahead of the November 1972 election. Fed funds rates fell from ~9% (mid-1969) to ~3.3% (early 1972); M1 growth accelerated to ~9% for 1972. Nixon won a 49-state landslide November 7 1972. The subsequent inflation: CPI ran ~3.2% in 1972, ~6.2% in 1973, ~11.0% in 1974 -- the beginning of the STAGFLATION decade Volcker would eventually crush. T3: the ALAN GREENSPAN -- GEORGE W. BUSH case, 2003-04. Greenspan cut the Fed funds rate to 1.00% by June 2003 (its lowest since 1958) and held it there until June 30 2004 -- when the FOMC finally began a slow tightening cycle right after the summer conventions and before the November 2004 election. Bush won reelection November 2 2004. Housing prices, buoyed by the extended low-rate environment, peaked in 2006; the 2008 GFC followed. The AUSTRIAN BUSINESS CYCLE THEORY reading of this sequence (Roger Garrison, 'Time and Money' 2001; Mark Thornton contemporaneously) predicted the housing bubble in real time. name: Medical licensing: Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom chapter 9
scope: The oldest and cleanest applied-Stigler-plus-Olson case: state-enforced professional cartels. T1: MILTON FRIEDMAN'S 'CAPITALISM AND FREEDOM' (University of Chicago Press 1962) CHAPTER 9, 'OCCUPATIONAL LICENSURE,' is the foundational modern critique of state medical licensing. Friedman argued state licensing of physicians -- typically enforced by the state MEDICAL BOARD, staffed largely by physicians themselves -- serves LESS to protect patients than to RESTRICT ENTRY into the profession, raising physician incomes and reducing patient access to lower-cost care. T2: the SPECIFIC MECHANISM Friedman named: the AMERICAN MEDICAL ASSOCIATION-influenced FLEXNER REPORT (1910, Abraham Flexner for the Carnegie Foundation) recommended shutting down non-Johns-Hopkins-model medical schools. Between 1904 and 1935 the number of US medical schools fell from 160 to 76; enrollment fell correspondingly. The AMA gained approval authority over medical schools via the LCME. Physician incomes rose relative to comparable professions across this period. T3: the CONTEMPORARY EVIDENCE. STUDIES BY MORRIS KLEINER (University of Minnesota) including 'LICENSING OCCUPATIONS: ENSURING QUALITY OR RESTRICTING COMPETITION?' (Upjohn Institute 2006) and Kleiner-Krueger 'Analyzing the Extent and Influence of Occupational Licensing on the Labor Market' (Journal of Labor Economics 2013) find that OCCUPATIONAL LICENSING has expanded from covering ~5% of the US workforce in 1950 to ~25% today, raising licensed-worker wages by ~15% on average -- with LITTLE MEASURABLE EFFECT on service quality. Medicine's specific case remains the deepest and most restrictive. T4: NURSE-PRACTITIONER + PHYSICIAN-ASSISTANT SCOPE-OF-PRACTICE laws are the modern empirical laboratory. States that allow full-practice authority for NPs (~26 states in 2024) see lower primary-care prices and no measurable quality difference from physician-only states, per multiple studies including the RAND Corporation's work and the American Association of Nurse Practitioners' meta-analyses. State medical societies routinely oppose scope expansion; state nursing associations support it -- a textbook OLSON concentrated-benefit-vs-concentrated-benefit interest-group struggle where PATIENTS (the dispersed interest) are absent from the negotiation. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: state PROFESSIONAL LICENSING is not primarily a quality-assurance mechanism -- it is a STATE-ENFORCED CARTEL, in which the licensed profession WRITES ITS OWN entry rules through capture of the licensing board. This is the STIGLER-CAPTURE + OLSON-CONCENTRATED-BENEFIT pattern in its most institutionally-formal form. The reasoning move: when a licensing board is populated by members of the licensed profession, DEFAULT SUSPICION is that entry restrictions serve incumbent income more than public safety. Friedman's practical proposal (Chapter 9) was CERTIFICATION rather than LICENSING -- the state may certify credentials, but should not forbid non-certified practitioners from offering services to informed adults. Further rungs: the CERTIFICATE OF NEED (CON) laws in 34 states requiring state approval before a hospital or clinic may add beds or equipment -- another cartel-preservation mechanism; the CLARK V. OKLAHOMA DENTAL BOARD line of federal antitrust cases (culminating in NORTH CAROLINA STATE BOARD OF DENTAL EXAMINERS v FTC, Supreme Court 2015) which held that state licensing boards ARE subject to federal antitrust review when they act as industry-member majorities without active state supervision.

name: Bootleggers and Baptists in the modern era: marijuana, EV mandates, online sales tax
scope: The applied-Yandle ladder for three modern regulatory battles where a moralist coalition and a commercial coalition ended up on the same side. T1: BRUCE YANDLE'S 1983 REGULATION MAGAZINE ESSAY 'BOOTLEGGERS AND BAPTISTS -- THE EDUCATION OF A REGULATORY ECONOMIST' named the pattern from PROHIBITION-ERA SUNDAY-CLOSING LAWS: BAPTISTS supported them on moral grounds (no alcohol sales on the Sabbath); BOOTLEGGERS supported them because closed legal outlets on Sundays meant every Sunday drinker had to buy from the illegal supplier. The two coalitions had opposite justifications and identical policy positions. T2: MARIJUANA LEGALIZATION as the modern case. When a state moves to legalize adult recreational cannabis, the resulting REGULATORY STRUCTURE (limited licenses, high excise taxes, capital + compliance requirements shutting out small growers) is repeatedly negotiated by an unlikely coalition -- ANTI-DRUG advocates (Baptists) accepting legalization only with heavy restrictions, and LARGE ESTABLISHED CANNABIS FIRMS + BIG-ALCOHOL companies (Bootleggers) supporting the same restrictions because they SHUT OUT small competitors. California, Illinois, and New York's rollouts have all shown this pattern; the illegal cannabis market in California in 2023 was still estimated at ~two-thirds of total consumption (CORROBORATE AT BUILD -- California DCC / New Frontier Data), preserved by the high-tax + limited-license structure. T3: EV MANDATES + zero-emission-vehicle rules as the automotive case. CLIMATE ADVOCATES (Baptists) supported California's Advanced Clean Cars II regulation (August 2022) mandating 100% zero-emission new vehicle sales by 2035. LARGE INCUMBENT AUTOMAKERS (Bootleggers -- GM, Ford, Stellantis) also supported it because they have the capital to comply and it forecloses smaller ICE competitors; SMALLER AUTOMAKERS and independent parts suppliers who cannot afford the transition timeline are the unrepresented losers. T4: ONLINE SALES TAX as the retail case. WAYFAIR v SOUTH DAKOTA (Supreme Court June 21 2018) allowed states to require out-of-state online sellers to collect sales tax. FISCAL CONSERVATIVES + STATE REVENUE OFFICIALS (Baptists) supported it on 'level playing field' + revenue grounds; BIG-BOX RETAILERS + AMAZON (Bootleggers -- who already had physical nexus and thus already collected tax) supported it because it raised compliance costs disproportionately on smaller Etsy/eBay-scale competitors. Post-Wayfair complexity has meant small e-commerce businesses now navigate 45+ state sales-tax regimes -- exactly the moat the incumbent retailers wanted. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: the STATED JUSTIFICATION of a regulation (moral, safety, environmental, fairness) is rarely a complete explanation of WHY IT PASSES. Look at WHO ORGANIZES to SUPPORT the specific detail-level rules, and you will find a coalition of MORAL ADVOCATES and COMMERCIAL BENEFICIARIES on the same side. YANDLE'S 2014 book with ADAM SMITH (the political scientist, not the 18th-century economist), 'BOOTLEGGERS AND BAPTISTS' (Cato Institute 2014), collects modern cases including bank regulation, environmental rules, and tobacco settlements. The reasoning move for policy analysis: when you see a UNUSUAL COALITION supporting a specific rule, follow the incentives -- there is almost always a concentrated commercial beneficiary hiding behind the moral advocate. Further rungs: the TOBACCO MASTER SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT 1998 as the archetypal case (public-health advocates + Big Four tobacco companies both wanted the settlement, which locked in Big Four market share by making entry expensive); DODD-FRANK 2010 large-bank support (as covered in p2) as the same pattern in banking.

name: NIMBY political economy: Palo Alto zoning as concentrated benefit
scope: Applied concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost analysis for local housing politics. T1: 'NIMBY' -- NOT IN MY BACKYARD -- describes the political pattern in which existing local homeowners organize successfully to block new housing development in their neighborhoods, even when the region's overall housing shortage produces high rents, long commutes, and displaced workers. The paradigm case: SILICON VALLEY, where extreme housing scarcity coexists with the world's highest concentration of tech-industry wealth. T2: PALO ALTO, CALIFORNIA, home to Stanford University and the historical center of Silicon Valley, has a MEDIAN HOME PRICE approaching $3 MILLION (2024, Zillow / CoreLogic). Approximately 94% of the city's residential land is zoned for SINGLE-FAMILY DETACHED HOMES; apartment construction has been effectively frozen for decades. Every proposed multi-family project faces years of hearings, environmental review, and neighbor opposition. The city added FEWER THAN 200 new housing units per year through much of the 2010s (CORROBORATE AT BUILD -- ABAG / RHNA figures) while adding tens of thousands of jobs. T3: the ECONOMIC ANALYSIS. EDWARD GLAESER (Harvard) and JOSEPH GYOURKO (Wharton), most notably in 'THE IMPACT OF ZONING ON HOUSING AFFORDABILITY' (NBER Working Paper 8835, 2002) and continuing work, estimate the ZONING TAX -- the wedge between the actual price of housing in constrained cities and its unconstrained construction cost -- runs 30-60% in Bay Area cities. That wedge is a pure TRANSFER from would-be residents to existing homeowners; the total capitalized wealth transfer to Bay Area single-family homeowners from restrictive zoning runs into the TRILLIONS of dollars. T4: the PUBLIC-CHOICE STRUCTURE that produces this. Existing PALO ALTO HOMEOWNERS are a CONCENTRATED BENEFICIARY GROUP -- they attend city council meetings, know the planning process, hire land-use attorneys, and vote in every local election. WOULD-BE RESIDENTS (workers priced out to Modesto, Sacramento, Reno, or out of California entirely) are a DISPERSED VICTIM GROUP -- they do not vote in Palo Alto, cannot attend Palo Alto hearings, and often do not know a specific project would have housed them. This is OLSON 1965 concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost, applied at the municipal scale, producing the housing shortage as its predicted output. T5: the YIMBY (YES-IN-MY-BACKYARD) COUNTER-COALITION emerged around 2015-16 as an attempt to organize the DISPERSED interest -- national groups like YIMBY ACTION, California-specific bills like SB 9 (2021, allowing duplexes on single-family lots), SB 35 (2017, streamlining approval of infill housing) and Minneapolis 2040 plan (2018, eliminating single-family zoning citywide) as jurisdictions attempting to restructure the rule-selection game. The RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: whenever a POLICY IS BADLY DAMAGING to a REGION'S ECONOMY, ask WHO SPECIFICALLY BENEFITS at the concentrated end -- the answer is often existing incumbent asset-holders whose wealth was created by the policy's restriction. Further rungs: SAN FRANCISCO'S SIMILAR ZONING pattern (widely covered by JASON FURMAN's economists' reports); the JAPANESE HOUSING SYSTEM as the international contrast (national zoning categories, comparatively free permitting, stable real housing prices in Tokyo despite metropolitan-area growth); the AUSTIN, TEXAS 2019-24 supply boom driving actual rent DECLINES as a US contrast case.

name: Welfare cliffs: the effective marginal tax rate that traps low-income households
scope: Applied incentive-analysis for the antipoverty policy stack. T1: a WELFARE CLIFF is the point on the income distribution where an additional dollar of EARNED WAGES triggers the LOSS of one or more MEANS-TESTED BENEFITS (Medicaid, SNAP food stamps, CHIP, housing assistance, EITC phase-outs, TANF, childcare subsidies, ACA premium subsidies). Because the lost benefits can exceed the additional wages, the EFFECTIVE MARGINAL TAX RATE facing the worker can approach or exceed 100%. T2: the CONCRETE PICTURE. Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta's CAREER LADDER IDENTIFIER AND FINANCIAL FORECASTER (CLIFF) tool, developed 2018-, allows household-specific mapping. A single mother of two in Illinois earning $30,000/year who receives a raise to $40,000/year can face a net loss of $2,000-$5,000 in total household resources after benefit phase-outs; the effective marginal tax rate on that raise can reach 110-130% in some benefit-stack configurations (Atlanta Fed CLIFF outputs -- CORROBORATE AT BUILD for specific state). T3: THOMAS SOWELL'S critique in 'THE VISION OF THE ANOINTED' (Basic Books 1995) documented that the pre-1965 African-American two-parent family rate was HIGHER than the white rate; the Great Society welfare expansion's phase-out structure penalized marriage (household income aggregation), employment (benefit loss), and savings (asset tests), producing exactly the family-structure and dependency outcomes the programs were nominally designed to alleviate. Sowell's move: 'judge policies by their RESULTS, not their INTENTIONS.' T4: the ACADEMIC EVIDENCE has caught up. STUDIES INCLUDING CASEY MULLIGAN'S 'THE REDISTRIBUTION RECESSION' (Oxford UP 2012) and the NATIONAL BUREAU OF ECONOMIC RESEARCH working-paper series (Chetty, Hendren, Katz, others) document that the safety-net + tax-credit interaction produces LOW-WAGE labor-supply distortions of magnitudes comparable to a 60-90% top-bracket income tax on the working poor -- larger than any tax faced by high-income households. The NATION'S ANTIPOVERTY SYSTEM effectively TAXES WORK ANY the exit from poverty. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: PROGRAMS designed to HELP a group can, through their PHASE-OUT INCENTIVE STRUCTURES, produce the OPPOSITE outcome. This is not a moral failing of program designers -- it is a mechanical consequence of stacking multiple means-tested benefits without coordinating their phase-out schedules. Milton Friedman's proposed alternative (Capitalism and Freedom 1962 ch 12) was the NEGATIVE INCOME TAX -- a single unified phase-out with a KNOWN, GRADUAL marginal rate -- which avoids the multi-program cliff by design. The reasoning move for policy analysis: WHENEVER an antipoverty program is expanded, ASK WHAT THE INTERACTION IS with the other 82 federal means-tested programs (Congressional Research Service count) already in place. Further rungs: the EARNED INCOME TAX CREDIT (EITC) established 1975 as the closest US approximation of Friedman's NIT idea, and its own phase-out kinks; the ACA PREMIUM-SUBSIDY CLIFF at 400% FPL (2014-21, temporarily removed 2021-25 by ARP + IRA) as the most recent famous individual cliff.

name: The Bennett hypothesis: federal student aid and the tuition it enables
scope: The applied seen-vs-unseen ladder for higher-education finance. T1: WILLIAM BENNETT, then US SECRETARY OF EDUCATION under Ronald Reagan, published 'OUR GREEDY COLLEGES' in the NEW YORK TIMES on FEBRUARY 18 1987 arguing that INCREASES IN FEDERAL FINANCIAL AID (Pell Grants, subsidized student loans) do not primarily reduce the net cost of college for students -- they primarily enable COLLEGES to raise tuition and capture the aid as revenue. The claim became known as the BENNETT HYPOTHESIS. T2: the AGGREGATE PATTERN. From 1978 to 2018, US average PUBLIC FOUR-YEAR TUITION rose approximately 213% in real terms; PRIVATE FOUR-YEAR TUITION rose approximately 129% in real terms; overall US CPI rose approximately 250% in nominal terms over the same window. Total FEDERAL STUDENT LOAN debt grew from ~$100B (1990s) to ~$1.7T (2023). The correlation with expanded federal aid programs (the 1965 HEA reauthorizations, the 1992 direct loan program, the 2010 elimination of private-lender intermediation) is tight. T3: the CAUSAL EVIDENCE. GREY GORDON + AARON HEDLUND'S 'ACCOUNTING FOR THE RISE IN COLLEGE TUITION' (NBER Working Paper 21967, 2016; American Economic Journal 2020) built a structural model finding that FEDERAL AID EXPANSION explains APPROXIMATELY 106% of the observed 1987-2010 tuition rise -- essentially all of it, with a slight over-estimate that other model features offset. DAVID LUCCA, TAYLOR NADAULD, KAREN SHEN's NEW YORK FED STAFF REPORT 733 'CREDIT SUPPLY AND THE RISE IN COLLEGE TUITION' (2015, revised 2019) exploited discontinuities in federal loan limits and found that a $1 increase in subsidized federal student loans led to a $0.60 increase in sticker tuition -- a direct market-mechanism confirmation. T4: the THREE MECHANISMS by which aid drives tuition. (a) DEMAND EFFECT: aid raises what students can pay; colleges price accordingly. (b) BUREAUCRATIC EXPANSION: aid-driven revenue funds administrative growth (US higher-ed admin staff grew ~87% from 1987 to 2011 vs a 50% increase in students, per HANDS ON GENERAL ACCOUNTING OFFICE / Delta Cost Project) rather than instructional capacity. (c) SELECTIVE-SIGNALING competition: institutions compete on amenities and prestige, funded by tuition, not on price. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: a SUBSIDY TO A DEMAND-SIDE PARTY (student) can be substantially CAPTURED by the SUPPLY-SIDE PARTY (college) when the supply is CONSTRAINED and the demand is INELASTIC. The SEEN effect Congress intended (help students afford college) is real but small; the UNSEEN effect is a decades-long tuition-inflation escalator and $1.7T in accumulated student debt. The reasoning move for policy analysis: WHEN A SUBSIDY IS PROPOSED, ASK who has the market power to price against the newly-enhanced payment capacity. The same mechanism operates in HEALTH-CARE SUBSIDIES (insurance subsidies -> premium inflation), HOUSING SUBSIDIES (Section 8 vouchers -> landlord rent capture in tight markets), and FIRST-TIME HOMEBUYER TAX CREDITS (2008-10 credit largely captured in seller prices, per multiple studies). Further rungs: RICHARD VEDDER's 'GOING BROKE BY DEGREE' (AEI 2004) as an earlier synthesis; the current STUDENT-DEBT-FORGIVENESS debate as the political sequel to the tuition inflation the aid programs enabled; the GAINFUL EMPLOYMENT rule as an attempted supply-side response.
source: PRIMARY: William J. Bennett, 'Our Greedy Colleges' New York Times (February 18 1987); Grey Gordon + Aaron Hedlund, 'Accounting for the Rise in College Tuition' NBER Working Paper 21967 (Feb 2016); David Lucca, Taylor Nadauld, Karen Shen, 'Credit Supply and the Rise in College Tuition' Federal Reserve Bank of New York Staff Report 733 (July 2015, revised Feb 2019). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Bennett hypothesis', 'Student loans in the United States', 'Tuition inflation', 'William Bennett' (2026-09-05) -- Bennett 1987 NYT article, tuition inflation 1978-2018 real percentages, Gordon-Hedlund 2016 structural model finding ~106% explanation, Lucca-Nadauld-Shen 2015 $0.60-per-$1 pass-through, US higher-ed admin staff growth 87% (1987-2011) per Delta Cost Project. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact Lucca-Nadauld-Shen pass-through coefficient; exact Gordon-Hedlund attribution percentage; exact administrative-staff growth figure from Delta Cost Project.
framing_note: The applied seen-vs-unseen ladder for the biggest single financial mistake of a generation of American parents. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (a NY Fed study found $0.60 of every $1 in extra federal student loan capacity became added tuition) and T4 (admin staff up 87% while student count rose 50% -- the aid built bureaucracy, not classrooms). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on Bennett writing in the NYT on a specific date in 1987, not 'define student aid.' BASTIAT PATTERN check: T5 is direct SEEN-vs-UNSEEN + INCENTIVE RECOGNITION -- who has pricing power when demand-side subsidies expand. RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT (LOAD-BEARING): the answer names the reasoning MOVE (Bennett hypothesis / subsidy capture by supply side, seen-vs-unseen at aggregate level, market-power pricing analysis) or the NAMED STUDY / CRITIC, NEVER 'student loans are bad' or 'colleges are greedy.' The ladder analyzes the STRUCTURAL PRICE MECHANISM. ACCURACY RAIL: the Gordon-Hedlund 106% attribution is a structural-model estimate; note the model dependency. Not every dollar of subsidy is captured in every market -- the ladder should present the mechanism, not overstate certainty. Bennett is the historical figure of the claim; Grey Gordon (Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond) and Lucca et al are the modern academic evidence. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: if the stem describes tuition rising as aid expanded, the answer is not 'tuition went up' (restatement) -- it is the NAMED HYPOTHESIS (Bennett hypothesis 1987), the NAMED STUDY (Lucca-Nadauld-Shen NY Fed 733, Gordon-Hedlund NBER 21967), or the NAMED MECHANISM (demand-subsidy capture by pricing-power supply). DISTRACTOR MINE: other named reasoning moves (Olson concentrated-benefits, Stigler capture, Sowell results-not-intentions), other subsidy-capture cases (health insurance premium inflation, Section 8 rent capture, homebuyer tax credit), other 1980s Reagan-era officials (Alan Greenspan, David Stockman, Donald Regan). name: The Farm Bill and SNAP: urban-rural logrolling
scope: The applied-Buchanan logrolling ladder for the largest recurring US authorization. T1: the US FARM BILL is a comprehensive multi-title statute reauthorized approximately every 5 years (recent iterations: 2002, 2008, 2014, 2018, 2024). Its combined cost is roughly $1.5 TRILLION over the 2024-2033 window per CONGRESSIONAL BUDGET OFFICE score. It funds crop insurance, commodity subsidies, conservation reserves, rural development, and -- as its LARGEST SINGLE COMPONENT -- the SUPPLEMENTAL NUTRITION ASSISTANCE PROGRAM (SNAP, formerly food stamps). T2: the SPENDING BREAKDOWN. In the 2018 Farm Bill, SNAP consumed approximately 76% of total 10-year projected spending; farm commodity programs consumed approximately 7%; crop insurance approximately 9%; conservation programs approximately 7% (CBO scoring, CORROBORATE AT BUILD). The vast majority of the 'Farm Bill' is not farm spending -- it is nutrition assistance for urban and suburban households, ~42 million recipients as of 2023. T3: the COALITION LOGIC that keeps the two together. URBAN AND SUBURBAN DEMOCRATS have the votes for SNAP but not for farm subsidies. RURAL REPUBLICANS have the votes for farm subsidies but not for SNAP. BUNDLED IN A SINGLE BILL, each side votes for the other side's priorities to secure its own -- textbook LOGROLLING as analyzed by JAMES BUCHANAN + GORDON TULLOCK in 'THE CALCULUS OF CONSENT' (Michigan 1962), where the authors identified logrolling as the vote-trading mechanism that allows policies to pass that neither would pass alone. T4: the HISTORICAL SEQUENCE. FOOD STAMPS were formally added to the USDA's portfolio in the FOOD STAMP ACT of 1964 (Lyndon Johnson, part of the Great Society). BEGINNING in 1973 they were EXPLICITLY BUNDLED with the Agriculture and Consumer Protection Act -- REPRESENTATIVE ROBERT DOLE (R-KS) and REPRESENTATIVE GEORGE McGOVERN (D-SD) architected the ongoing bundling as a permanent coalition device. Every farm-bill reauthorization since has kept the bundle. Every recent proposal to SEPARATE SNAP from the farm titles (e.g., the 2013 House proposal to strip SNAP out) has failed -- because separation destroys the bipartisan coalition each half needs to pass. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: WHENEVER two policies that seem thematically unrelated are STATUTORILY BUNDLED, the DEFAULT EXPLANATION is that the bundle exists to build a majority coalition NEITHER HALF could assemble alone. This is not corruption -- it is Buchanan-Tullock logrolling operating as designed. The DIAGNOSTIC QUESTION: what happens to the voting coalition if you unbundle the statute? If it collapses, the bundle IS the reason both halves pass. The same pattern appears in OMNIBUS APPROPRIATIONS BILLS, EMERGENCY-SPENDING PACKAGES (defense + disaster relief), and MUST-PASS DEFENSE AUTHORIZATION BILLS (NDAA) that accumulate unrelated riders. Further rungs: the CHRISTMAS-TREE BILL tradition of adding riders in conference; the LINE-ITEM VETO ACT 1996 that would have let presidents strike individual provisions -- struck down by CLINTON v CITY OF NEW YORK (Supreme Court June 25 1998) as unconstitutional; VETO POINTS in political-science literature (George Tsebelis) as the formal analysis of what logrolling exploits.
source: PRIMARY: James M. Buchanan + Gordon Tullock, 'The Calculus of Consent' (Michigan 1962) esp. chapters on logrolling and vote-trading; Farm Bill 2018 (Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018, P.L. 115-334); Congressional Budget Office score of Farm Bill 2018 (May 2018). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'United States farm bill', 'Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program', 'Food Stamp Act of 1964', 'Agriculture and Consumer Protection Act of 1973', 'Logrolling', 'Clinton v City of New York' (2026-09-05) -- Farm Bill 5-year reauthorization cadence, ~$1.5T 10-year cost, SNAP ~76% of Farm Bill spending, ~42M SNAP recipients, Food Stamp Act 1964, 1973 farm-bill SNAP bundling by Dole + McGovern, 2013 House SNAP-separation attempt, Line-Item Veto Act 1996 + Clinton v NYC 1998. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact CBO 2018 Farm Bill title-share percentages; exact current SNAP recipient count and average benefit.
framing_note: The applied Buchanan-Tullock logrolling ladder made concrete. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the 'Farm Bill' is 76% food stamps -- not farm spending at all) and T3 (urban Democrats and rural Republicans have the votes for each other's priorities but not their own -- so they trade, and the bundle passes). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on the 5-year reauthorization cadence, not 'define logrolling.' BASTIAT PATTERN check: T5 is direct INCENTIVE RECOGNITION -- what happens to the voting coalition if you unbundle? RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT (LOAD-BEARING): the answer names the reasoning MOVE (Buchanan-Tullock logrolling, coalition-building via bundling, unbundling-collapses-coalition diagnostic) or the NAMED STATUTE / ARCHITECT, NEVER 'the Farm Bill is corrupt' or 'SNAP is bad.' The ladder is neutral on whether farm subsidies and SNAP are good policies; it analyzes the MECHANISM by which they persist together. ACCURACY RAIL: Dole-McGovern bundling architecture in 1973 is documented; exact roles should be verified. The 2013 House SNAP separation attempt actually PASSED the House on party lines but failed in conference -- present the outcome carefully. Clinton v NYC 1998 is real and correctly cited. DISTRACTOR MINE: other named public-choice concepts (Olson concentrated-benefit, Stigler capture, Niskanen budget-max), other omnibus-bundling cases (NDAA riders, CROMNIBUS 2014, omnibus appropriations), other 1960s Great Society programs (Medicare 1965, Head Start 1965). name: Ex-Im Bank and Boeing: the concentrated federal lending case
scope: The applied-Olson ladder for federal export lending. T1: the EXPORT-IMPORT BANK OF THE UNITED STATES (Ex-Im Bank) is a federal agency established by Franklin Roosevelt via Executive Order 6581 on FEBRUARY 2 1934, providing loans, loan guarantees, and export credit insurance to foreign buyers of US-manufactured goods. T2: the CONCENTRATION PATTERN. According to MERCATUS CENTER analysis (Veronique de Rugy + others, 2014-2015) of Ex-Im Bank filings, from 2007 to 2013 BOEING was the SINGLE LARGEST BENEFICIARY of Ex-Im Bank support, receiving approximately 40% of ALL Ex-Im Bank loan and guarantee volume. Ten large firms (Boeing, General Electric, Caterpillar, and others) received the majority of Ex-Im's support; small exporters, in whose name the agency is politically defended, receive a small share. T3: the 2015 LAPSE. The Ex-Im Bank's charter lapsed on JUNE 30 2015 when Congress declined to renew it -- a rare successful mobilization of the DISPERSED interest against a CONCENTRATED-BENEFIT program, largely orchestrated by CONSERVATIVE HERITAGE FOUNDATION + CLUB FOR GROWTH + FREEDOMWORKS coalitions. The bank was UN-authorized for financing new deals for approximately five months. Its charter was renewed in DECEMBER 2015 as part of a highway-bill omnibus (Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act) -- exactly the Buchanan-Tullock logrolling mechanism the ladder above describes. T4: what HAPPENED during the lapse tested the standard defense of the program (that Ex-Im is essential for US export competitiveness). US EXPORTS did not measurably decline; Boeing continued to sell aircraft to foreign buyers (using commercial bank financing at slightly higher spreads); the counterfactual case for the bank's necessity was weaker than its proponents had claimed. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: OLSON'S 'THE LOGIC OF COLLECTIVE ACTION' (Harvard 1965) predicted exactly this pattern -- a program providing large concentrated benefits to a small number of large firms will attract intense organized lobbying from those firms (Boeing spent millions annually lobbying to preserve Ex-Im), while the dispersed cost to taxpayers, competitor US firms, and foreign consumers is not organized against it. The 2015 LAPSE was the RARE moment when the dispersed interest actually organized enough to win -- and even then, only for five months before the bundling mechanism restored the bank. The reasoning move: WHENEVER a federal credit or subsidy program is defended in the name of 'small firms' or 'general competitiveness,' ASK WHAT PERCENTAGE of the actual dollar volume goes to a small number of large firms. That percentage is a direct measurement of the concentration Olson predicted. Further rungs: the OVERSEAS PRIVATE INVESTMENT CORPORATION (OPIC, renamed DFC in 2019) as a parallel concentrated-benefit vehicle; the SMALL BUSINESS ADMINISTRATION (SBA) 7(a) loan program showing a similar though less extreme concentration among the largest SBA-eligible firms.
source: PRIMARY: Mancur Olson, 'The Logic of Collective Action' (Harvard 1965); Veronique de Rugy, 'Reforming the Export-Import Bank' Mercatus Working Paper (2014); Export-Import Bank Reauthorization Act of 2015 (Title VI of the FAST Act, P.L. 114-94, December 4 2015). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Export-Import Bank of the United States', 'Boeing', 'Overseas Private Investment Corporation' (2026-09-05) -- Ex-Im founded by EO 6581 Feb 2 1934, Boeing ~40% of Ex-Im loan/guarantee volume 2007-13, charter lapse June 30 2015, reauthorization in FAST Act December 4 2015, OPIC renamed to DFC 2019 via BUILD Act. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact Boeing share of Ex-Im volume for a specific year; exact FAST Act signing date.
framing_note: The applied-Olson ladder made concrete with a beloved 90-year-old federal agency. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (a single company, Boeing, received ~40% of ALL Ex-Im Bank support -- the 'Small Business Administration of aerospace') and T4 (during the five-month 2015 lapse, US exports did not measurably decline -- the program's defenders had overstated its necessity). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on FDR signing EO 6581 in 1934, not 'define export credit.' BASTIAT PATTERN check: T5 is direct OLSON INCENTIVE RECOGNITION on the concentration-vs-dispersion asymmetry. RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT (LOAD-BEARING): the answer names the reasoning MOVE (Olson concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost, single-beneficiary-percentage diagnostic) or the NAMED PROGRAM / EVENT, NEVER 'abolish Ex-Im' or 'Boeing is bad.' The ladder analyzes the CONCENTRATION PATTERN, which is a factual matter. ACCURACY RAIL: Boeing's ~40% share is documented for the 2007-13 window in Mercatus analysis; do not extrapolate uncritically to other years. The 2015 lapse was real; the counterfactual on export effects is estimated from short-window data and should be presented as such. DISTRACTOR MINE: other named public-choice concepts (Stigler capture, Buchanan logrolling, Tullock rent-seeking), other federal credit programs (SBA 7(a), USDA rural development lending, DFC formerly OPIC), other 1934 Roosevelt agencies (SEC, FCC, National Labor Relations Board). name: Sports-stadium subsidies: the economists' near-consensus
scope: The applied concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost ladder for the most-studied US local-policy transfer. T1: US STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS have spent tens of billions of dollars over recent decades on subsidies for PROFESSIONAL SPORTS STADIUMS -- through tax-exempt bonds, direct construction grants, tax abatements, and infrastructure investments. The typical modern NFL or MLB stadium project involves several hundred million to over a billion dollars in public contribution. T2: the ACADEMIC LITERATURE'S NEAR-UNANIMOUS FINDING. DENNIS COATES + BRAD HUMPHREYS'S extensive body of work, most notably 'THE ECONOMIC IMPACT OF POSTSEASON PLAY IN PROFESSIONAL SPORTS' (Journal of Sports Economics 2002) and their METHODOLOGY-SURVEY 'DO ECONOMISTS REACH A CONCLUSION ON SUBSIDIES FOR SPORTS FRANCHISES, STADIUMS, AND MEGA-EVENTS?' (Econ Journal Watch 2008), reviewed dozens of independent studies and found NEAR-UNANIMOUS professional-economist agreement that publicly-subsidized stadiums do NOT generate positive net economic effects for the host region -- sports spending substitutes for other local entertainment spending; the multiplier effects claimed by boosters are systematically overestimated. T3: the CONCRETE MECHANISM. A family that spends $200 at a baseball game does not usually create new economic activity -- they spend $200 that would otherwise have gone to a restaurant, a movie, a bowling alley. The visible sports-arena employment is real; the LESS-VISIBLE lost restaurant, movie, bowling employment is the offset. BASTIAT would recognize this immediately as SEEN-vs-UNSEEN. Meanwhile the CONCENTRATED beneficiary is the TEAM OWNER, whose franchise value rises substantially when public capital funds the stadium and the owner captures the ticket, concession, and media revenue. T4: WHY THE SUBSIDIES PERSIST despite the academic consensus. TEAM OWNERS are a CONCENTRATED BENEFICIARY -- typically billionaires with the resources to hire lobbyists, fund political campaigns, and threaten to relocate to a competing city. TAXPAYERS are a DISPERSED COST -- the per-household burden ($100-$500) is too small to motivate individual political engagement. Cities also face a PRISONER'S-DILEMMA structure: any single city that refuses to subsidize loses its team to a rival city that will subsidize, so the coalition of cities finds it individually rational to overpay even though collective rationality would say no. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: WHEN academic experts on a policy question reach NEAR-UNANIMOUS agreement that a policy has negative net effects, and the policy nonetheless PERSISTS UNIVERSALLY, the explanation is almost always CONCENTRATED-BENEFIT / DISPERSED-COST public-choice combined with a JURISDICTIONAL PRISONER'S DILEMMA. This is not a failure of democracy per se -- it is a predictable consequence of the incentive structure Olson identified in 1965. The reasoning move for policy analysis: SEEK THE PROFESSIONAL CONSENSUS on effects; if the consensus is that the policy is negative and the policy persists, LOOK FOR CONCENTRATED BENEFICIARIES with organizational advantages. Further rungs: the ARLINGTON, TEXAS Cowboys Stadium (opened 2009, ~$325M public share); the LAS VEGAS RAIDERS Allegiant Stadium (opened 2020, ~$750M public share via hotel-room tax); the FEDERAL TAX-EXEMPT BOND SUBSIDY that lowered municipal borrowing cost across every stadium project 1986-2017, estimated at $3B+ cumulative federal cost per Brookings analysis.
source: PRIMARY: Dennis Coates + Brad Humphreys, 'Do Economists Reach a Conclusion on Subsidies for Sports Franchises, Stadiums, and Mega-Events?' Econ Journal Watch 5 no 3 (Sept 2008); Coates + Humphreys, 'The Economic Impact of Postseason Play in Professional Sports' Journal of Sports Economics 3 no 3 (2002); Ted Gayer + Alexander Gold + Austin Drukker, 'Tax-Exempt Municipal Bonds and the Financing of Professional Sports Stadiums' Brookings (2016). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Stadium subsidy', 'Dennis Coates', 'Brad Humphreys', 'AT&T Stadium', 'Allegiant Stadium' (2026-09-05) -- Coates-Humphreys 2008 Econ Journal Watch survey finding near-unanimous negative-effect consensus, Brookings 2016 estimate of $3B+ cumulative federal tax-exempt bond subsidy to stadiums 1986-2017, Cowboys Stadium 2009 with ~$325M public share, Allegiant Stadium Vegas 2020 with ~$750M public share. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact Brookings cumulative federal-subsidy estimate; exact public share for the specific stadiums cited.

Dinner-test payoff: T2 (essentially every independent economist who studies this concludes stadium subsidies don't produce net positive local effects -- and cities pay them anyway) and T4 (billionaire team owner + relocation threat + prisoner's dilemma among cities = subsidies persist despite the consensus). SCENE-LED: T1 opens on the aggregate spending scale, not 'define subsidy.' BASTIAT PATTERN check: T3 hits SEEN-vs-UNSEEN directly; T4 is direct OLSON INCENTIVE RECOGNITION; T5 is the meta-diagnostic. Team owners are legal actors playing the game the incentive structure sets up. name: Public-sector unions: FDR's warning and Wisconsin Act 10
scope: The applied-Olson ladder for public-sector collective bargaining. T1: FRANKLIN D. ROOSEVELT, no enemy of PRIVATE-sector unions (the Wagner Act 1935 gave them their strongest federal protections), wrote to LUTHER STEWARD, President of the National Federation of Federal Employees, on AUGUST 16 1937 that 'the process of collective bargaining, as usually understood, CANNOT BE TRANSPLANTED into the public service' -- because the counterparty across the bargaining table in a private-sector negotiation (a profit-maximizing employer) is REPLACED in a public-sector negotiation by (a taxpayer-funded employer whose ultimate check-writer is the same voter the union spends its dues to influence). Roosevelt considered a public-sector strike 'unthinkable and intolerable.' T2: the LEGAL PICTURE for the following seventy years. Federal employees remained largely unable to strike (Postal Reorganization Act 1970, Civil Service Reform Act 1978). But STATE and LOCAL public-sector unions grew substantially after the 1962 KENNEDY EXECUTIVE ORDER 10988 granting federal employees limited collective-bargaining rights and comparable state-level authorizations that followed. By 2010, public-sector union density (~36%) was more than four times private-sector density (~7%). T3: the WISCONSIN ACT 10 REFORM. In FEBRUARY-MARCH 2011, Governor SCOTT WALKER proposed and the Wisconsin legislature enacted Act 10, which sharply limited public-sector collective bargaining for most state and local employees (excluding police and firefighters), required union recertification annually, and ended automatic dues deduction. The bill passed after weeks of massive protest at the state capitol and a Democratic-Senator walkout to Illinois to deny quorum. It was upheld by the Wisconsin Supreme Court in JULY 2014. T4: the EMPIRICAL EFFECTS studied by economists including WILL FLANDERS (Wisconsin Institute for Law and Liberty) and by education-policy researchers examining teacher-quality effects. Wisconsin PUBLIC-SECTOR UNION MEMBERSHIP fell substantially (WEAC lost most of its members within a few years). Local governments and school districts gained flexibility to reform pension and health-benefit structures. Wisconsin's state pension liabilities improved relative to comparable states. Long-term academic outcomes (which the reform's critics predicted would suffer) showed mixed effects -- some studies found no negative effect, some found teacher-selection improvements as compensation structures became more meritocratic. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: FDR's insight identifies a UNIQUE incentive structure in public-sector unions -- the union spends dues on political campaigns that select the officials WHO NEGOTIATE with the union across the bargaining table. This is a CIRCLE that private-sector unions cannot close: private-sector union dues cannot select the CEO. The reasoning move for policy analysis: whenever an INTEREST GROUP spends resources both on POLITICAL INFLUENCE and on NEGOTIATION with a counterparty whose selection it partly determines, the standard bargaining-model logic breaks down; the interest group is effectively bargaining with itself. This is OLSON'S CONCENTRATED-BENEFIT insight combined with STIGLER'S CAPTURE insight in a single institutional structure. The ladder does NOT resolve the political question of whether public-sector collective bargaining should be permitted; it teaches the STRUCTURAL DIAGNOSIS FDR made in 1937 and that Wisconsin Act 10 attempted to address. Further rungs: the CALIFORNIA STATE EMPLOYEES' RETIREMENT SYSTEM (CalPERS) as a $460B fund whose unfunded pension liabilities remain a genuine fiscal concern; the JANUS v AFSCME Supreme Court decision (JUNE 27 2018) ending compulsory public-sector union agency fees for non-members.

framing_note: The applied-Olson ladder for what FDR himself flagged as a unique public-sector structural problem. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (FDR, the FRIEND of private-sector unions, said in 1937 that public-sector collective bargaining 'cannot be transplanted' from the private context) and T5 (public-sector unions spend dues to elect the officials who then sit across the table from them -- effectively bargaining with themselves). RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT (LOAD-BEARING): the answer names the reasoning MOVE (FDR's structural diagnosis, bargaining-with-oneself circle, Olson + Stigler in single institutional form) or the NAMED FIGURE / STATUTE, NEVER 'public unions are bad' or 'Walker was right.' name: Anti-price-gouging laws: Michael Munger, John Shepperson, and the ice truck
scope: The applied Hayekian-knowledge-problem + Bastiat ladder for disaster price controls. T1: MOST US STATES have ANTI-PRICE-GOUGING LAWS that prohibit selling essential goods (fuel, ice, generators, water, building materials) at 'unconscionably' elevated prices during declared emergencies. Penalties include fines, license suspension, and, in some states, criminal prosecution. The stated purpose: prevent exploitation of desperate disaster victims. T2: MICHAEL MUNGER (Duke University, formerly chair of political science) tells THE JOHN SHEPPERSON STORY in a widely-cited essay ('THEY CLAPPED: CAN PRICE GOUGING LAWS PROHIBIT SCARCITY?' Cato Unbound 2007). After HURRICANE FRANCES hit Florida in SEPTEMBER 2004, Shepperson (a Kentucky truck driver) bought 19 generators, rented a U-Haul, and drove 600 miles to hurricane-affected Florida, offering the generators for $1,000 each (roughly TWICE his cost). Florida police ARRESTED him under the state's anti-price-gouging statute, CONFISCATED the generators, and jailed him for four days. The generators sat in police custody, unused, while hurricane victims went without power. T3: what Shepperson actually did, in Hayekian terms: he moved SCARCE PHYSICAL CAPITAL (generators) from a low-value use (Kentucky, normal times) to a high-value use (post-hurricane Florida) using the PRICE SIGNAL as his coordination mechanism. The elevated Florida price told him the resources were desperately needed there; his willingness to make the trip depended on the elevated price making the effort worthwhile. Anti-gouging laws SEVER THIS PRICE SIGNAL and thereby PREVENT THE COORDINATION they claim to enable. The 'protection' from high prices IS the mechanism preventing supply from arriving. T4: this is HAYEK'S 1945 KNOWLEDGE-PROBLEM argument ('THE USE OF KNOWLEDGE IN SOCIETY,' American Economic Review) applied to disasters. No central emergency-management agency in Florida knew that a Kentucky truck driver had spare generators and could reach the affected area within days. The PRICE SIGNAL is how that dispersed knowledge got activated. When the state OUTLAWS the signal, it forecloses the flow of exactly the resources it claims to be protecting citizens' access to. Meanwhile, the SEEN effect (no one 'gouged') coexists with the UNSEEN cost (thousands of households in the dark for weeks). T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: PRICE CONTROLS during scarcity DO NOT CREATE ABUNDANCE -- they only rearrange the shortage and eliminate the incentive to alleviate it. The ETHICAL objection to 'gouging' rests on a picture of a static supply where a seller extracts surplus from desperate buyers. The REAL choice is between EXPENSIVE SUPPLY THAT ARRIVES and CHEAP SUPPLY THAT DOES NOT EXIST. The reasoning move for policy analysis: WHEN a regulation SEVERS A PRICE SIGNAL in a market with dispersed information, EXPECT the coordination that the price signal enabled to disappear. This is HAYEK 1945 as operative policy diagnosis. Further rungs: the 1970s GASOLINE PRICE CONTROLS producing gas lines (US) as the parallel case at national scale; RUSSELL SOBEL + PETER LEESON's work on disaster-relief economics documenting the WAL-MART post-KATRINA response (August-September 2005) as an unregulated-but-not-price-gouging supply-chain success; VENEZUELA under Maduro as the extreme case of price controls producing chronic shortage.
