name: Universal basic income: Milton Friedman's negative income tax vs Andrew Yang's UBI
scope: The applied incentive-analysis + Sowell-tradeoffs ladder for the two major cash-transfer proposals. T1: MILTON FRIEDMAN, in 'CAPITALISM AND FREEDOM' (Chicago 1962) CHAPTER 12, proposed the NEGATIVE INCOME TAX (NIT): a unified cash transfer that provides a minimum income to all households and phases out at a KNOWN, GRADUAL marginal rate -- replacing the tangled multi-program welfare stack with a single administratively-simple mechanism. Friedman's motivation was NOT ideological expansion of the safety net; it was ADMINISTRATIVE SIMPLIFICATION and PRESERVATION OF WORK INCENTIVES (via a gradual, transparent phase-out that would REPLACE the multiple cliffs of the existing programs). T2: the EMPIRICAL TEST. The NIT was tested in several LARGE-SCALE RANDOMIZED EXPERIMENTS in the US (New Jersey / Pennsylvania 1968-72, Seattle / Denver Income Maintenance Experiments 1970-77, others) and Canada (Manitoba MINCOME 1974-79). Findings: modest work-hour reductions (~5-13% for primary earners, larger for secondary earners and youth), some evidence of family-structure effects, but not the catastrophic labor-supply collapse critics had predicted. Substantial administrative-cost savings over the multi-program comparison were consistently documented. T3: the MODERN UBI PROPOSALS have moved BEYOND Friedman's NIT structure to a UNIVERSAL flat payment regardless of income -- no phase-out, no work test. ANDREW YANG'S 2020 presidential campaign centered on a 'FREEDOM DIVIDEND' of $1,000/month to every American adult, funded partly by a value-added tax; the SAM ALTMAN / OPENRESEARCH BASIC INCOME STUDY (2020-24, unconditional $1,000/month to 1,000 recipients in Illinois and Texas, published August 2024) provided the largest recent US RCT evidence, finding recipients reduced work hours by roughly 1.3-1.4 hours per week, modest health improvements, and no clear positive employment outcomes despite proponent hopes. T4: the KEY THEORETICAL CONTRAST between the two proposals. Friedman's NIT REPLACES the existing safety-net stack (with its 100%+ effective marginal tax rate cliffs); modern UBI adds a UNIVERSAL FLOOR on top of the existing system (with its higher gross cost). NIT preserves work incentives via gradual phase-out; UBI's incentive effect depends on whether the tax funding it applies phase-in effects at the same income levels. This is not a trivial technical difference -- Friedman would have supported REPLACING programs with a NIT and OPPOSED adding a UBI on top of them. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: WHENEVER two policies are described with similar labels ('cash transfer to the poor,' 'basic income'), ASK WHAT SPECIFIC INCENTIVE MECHANISM each design creates -- particularly the EFFECTIVE MARGINAL TAX RATE facing the recipient as income rises. Same-label proposals with DIFFERENT phase-out structures produce DIFFERENT behavioral outcomes. This is SOWELL'S 'THERE ARE NO SOLUTIONS, ONLY TRADEOFFS' applied at the design level: a UBI + existing safety net is not obviously better than an NIT-only structure; the tradeoffs run in different directions and depend on specific design parameters. The reasoning move for policy analysis: read the STATUTORY DESIGN, not the LABEL; two 'basic income' proposals can have opposite incentive properties. Further rungs: the ALASKA PERMANENT FUND DIVIDEND (annual per-capita oil-royalty payment since 1982, $1,000-$2,000/year typically) as the longest-running US universal cash-transfer program; the STOCKTON SEED (Stockton, California 2019-21) as an early city-scale UBI pilot; Charles MURRAY's 'IN OUR HANDS: A PLAN TO REPLACE THE WELFARE STATE' (AEI 2006) proposing a $10,000/adult UBI that REPLACES nearly all existing US welfare and social-insurance programs (a NIT-style structural move under a UBI label).

name: ESG as regulatory capture: BlackRock, Vanguard, State Street and the Big Three vote
scope: Applied capture analysis for the modern investor-stewardship debate. T1: ESG stands for ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL, GOVERNANCE -- a framework for evaluating corporate behavior against non-financial criteria. ESG-branded investment funds grew rapidly 2015-22 to peak around $20 TRILLION in nominal 'ESG assets under management' globally, though counting methodology is contested. T2: the CONCENTRATION at the top. Three US ASSET MANAGERS -- BLACKROCK (~$10T+ AUM), VANGUARD (~$8T+), and STATE STREET (~$4T+) -- collectively manage over $22 TRILLION and own approximately 20-25% of the shares of the average S&P 500 company (LUCIAN BEBCHUK + SCOTT HIRST, 'THE SPECTER OF THE GIANT THREE,' Boston University Law Review 2019). Because they PROXY-VOTE the shares in their index funds, the Big Three collectively cast approximately 25% of votes at most major US corporate meetings. T3: THE CAPTURE PATTERN. When BlackRock CEO LARRY FINK began issuing his ANNUAL CEO LETTERS calling for corporate action on climate, DEI, and other ESG issues (2018-22), the underlying mechanism was that BlackRock's proxy-voting policies gave it de facto influence over corporate boards without owning the shares beneficially. The individual retail retirement-account holders whose money is in BlackRock funds have no meaningful say in the proxy votes cast on their behalf. This is a form of REGULATORY-STYLE CAPTURE operating through PRIVATE FIDUCIARY infrastructure -- a small number of asset-manager decision-makers acting for tens of millions of dispersed principal shareholders. T4: THE POLITICAL BACKLASH began around 2022. FLORIDA GOVERNOR RON DESANTIS led state-level anti-ESG action starting with an August 2022 divestment of $2B in Florida state pension assets from BlackRock over ESG-voting concerns; a coalition of 19 state attorneys general filed comment letters and, in some cases, took similar divestment action. The federal Department of Labor's ERISA fiduciary-rule updates (2022, 2024) went in both directions across administrations. BlackRock itself began ADJUSTING its ESG-emphasis language starting 2023 and offered VOTING-CHOICE PROGRAMS (allowing large institutional clients to direct their own proxy votes) in what looked like a response to political pressure. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: CAPTURE is not only a story of GOVERNMENT REGULATORS being captured by regulated firms. It can operate through PRIVATE FIDUCIARY INFRASTRUCTURE when a small number of financial gatekeepers control voting rights on behalf of millions of dispersed principals whose preferences are neither known nor consulted. The reasoning move for policy analysis: WHENEVER a small number of intermediaries make decisions on behalf of many principals whose consent is inferred rather than solicited, ASK WHETHER the intermediaries' incentives align with the principals' interests -- and if not, EXPECT capture. THOMAS SOWELL'S 'COMPARED TO WHAT?' applies here too: 'ESG activism' compared to a passive-fund-manager-as-fiduciary alternative is a different question than 'corporate responsibility' compared to 'shareholder primacy.' The bank does NOT declare a policy verdict on ESG substance; it teaches the CAPTURE-STRUCTURE RECOGNITION. Further rungs: the 1970 MILTON FRIEDMAN NEW YORK TIMES MAGAZINE ESSAY 'THE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY OF BUSINESS IS TO INCREASE ITS PROFITS' as the founding statement of the shareholder-primacy position that ESG explicitly rejects; the CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, EU) as the parallel European regulatory push producing compliance costs on ~50,000+ companies from 2024.

name: NCAA amateurism as cartel: O'Bannon v NCAA 2014 and the 2021 NIL unwinding
scope: The applied-cartel-analysis ladder for college athletics. T1: the NATIONAL COLLEGIATE ATHLETIC ASSOCIATION (NCAA) governed roughly 500,000 US college athletes across ~1,100 member institutions. From its 1906 founding through 2021, the NCAA maintained AMATEURISM RULES prohibiting athletes from receiving any compensation beyond a scholarship, room, board, and small stipend -- while the SAME associations generated ~$18-19 BILLION in annual revenue in the peak years (2018-19), including multi-billion-dollar television contracts for the NCAA basketball tournament and college football playoffs. T2: economists have LONG identified the NCAA as a TEXTBOOK HORIZONTAL PRICE-FIXING CARTEL -- roughly 1,100 nominally-competing 'employers' (universities) collectively agreeing to fix the price of athlete labor at zero above their standardized in-kind compensation. In any other industry, such an agreement would be a per-se Sherman Act Section 1 violation. GARY BECKER, RODNEY FORT, ANDREW ZIMBALIST, and RONALD GILSON's academic work spanning 1970s-2010s treated NCAA amateurism as the case study in successful multi-decade cartel enforcement despite obvious cartel-instability incentives. T3: the LEGAL COLLAPSE began with O'BANNON v NCAA (Ninth Circuit August 8 2015, upholding partial district-court ruling of August 2014 by Judge Claudia Wilken) -- ED O'BANNON, a former UCLA basketball star, sued the NCAA over the use of his likeness in EA Sports college basketball video games without compensation. Wilken held that the NCAA's amateurism rules violated Sherman Section 1 as an unreasonable restraint of trade. The remedy was limited but the precedent was foundational. T4: NCAA v ALSTON (Supreme Court UNANIMOUS 9-0 decision June 21 2021) then affirmed that NCAA restrictions on education-related benefits also violated Sherman Section 1. JUSTICE BRETT KAVANAUGH'S concurrence explicitly signaled that the FULL amateurism structure was likely unconstitutional as a cartel. Under state-legislative and court-decision pressure, the NCAA formally allowed NAME IMAGE LIKENESS (NIL) compensation effective JULY 1 2021 -- a total unwinding of a century of amateurism. Within three years the NIL market was estimated at $1B+ annually flowing to college athletes from third-party endorsements. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: A CARTEL, EVEN A LONG-STANDING AND CULTURALLY-DEFENDED ONE, cannot indefinitely suppress prices for a factor of production whose market value substantially exceeds the fixed price. The 'AMATEURISM' framing was a JUSTIFICATION for the underlying cartel structure; the moment courts began looking at the structure through standard antitrust lenses, the whole edifice collapsed rapidly. The reasoning move for policy analysis: WHENEVER an industry-wide arrangement fixes the price of an input at a level far below the value it produces, ASK WHAT LEGAL OR CULTURAL PROP prevents the cartel from breaking down -- and expect that prop to erode over time. BUCHANAN'S 'POLITICS WITHOUT ROMANCE' applies here too: the 'noble amateurism' rhetoric of the NCAA obscured a straightforward economic-organization pattern. Further rungs: the HOUSE v NCAA settlement (approved June 6 2025) creating a revenue-sharing framework and effectively completing the transition to college athletes as compensated labor; the 1976 NBA-ABA merger + the 1984 NCAA v BOARD OF REGENTS decision (Supreme Court freed schools from NCAA television-contract restrictions) as earlier stages of the same unwinding.

name: Kelo v City of New London 2005: eminent domain and public choice
scope: The applied rent-seeking + property-rights ladder from a single infamous Supreme Court case. T1: SUSETTE KELO owned a small pink house at 8 East Street in the Fort Trumbull neighborhood of NEW LONDON, CONNECTICUT. She had bought and renovated it as her dream home. In the late 1990s the City of New London, working with the New London Development Corporation, adopted a redevelopment plan to build offices, retail, and residential development around a new $300M Pfizer research campus. Kelo's house sat in the plan's footprint. She refused to sell. T2: the city moved to seize her property through EMINENT DOMAIN under the FIFTH AMENDMENT'S TAKINGS CLAUSE, which permits taking private property for 'PUBLIC USE' with just compensation. Historically 'public use' meant roads, schools, military installations -- direct government uses. The New London taking was different: it was a PRIVATE-TO-PRIVATE transfer, from Kelo (private homeowner) to a private developer, for the ECONOMIC-DEVELOPMENT BENEFIT the city projected the redevelopment would produce. T3: the case reached the US Supreme Court as KELO v CITY OF NEW LONDON, decided JUNE 23 2005. In a 5-4 DECISION (JUSTICE JOHN PAUL STEVENS writing for the majority; JUSTICE SANDRA DAY O'CONNOR writing the principal dissent joined by REHNQUIST, THOMAS, and SCALIA), the Court held that ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT satisfies the 'public use' requirement of the Fifth Amendment. Justice O'Connor's dissent: 'The specter of condemnation hangs over all property. Nothing is to prevent the State from replacing any Motel 6 with a Ritz-Carlton, any home with a shopping mall, or any farm with a factory.' T4: the AFTERMATH. The Kelo redevelopment PROJECT FAILED. Pfizer closed its New London research facility in 2009-10; the cleared land where Kelo's house and her neighbors' homes had stood remained VACANT for over a decade. Kelo's pink house itself was moved to a new location. Following the decision, 45 STATES enacted CONSTITUTIONAL OR STATUTORY REFORMS restricting private-to-private eminent domain takings for economic development, largely driven by campaigns from the INSTITUTE FOR JUSTICE (Kelo's counsel) documenting concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost patterns in similar cases nationwide. T5: the RECOGNITION-MOVE this teaches: the KELO decision, on its face, was about the meaning of 'public use' in the Fifth Amendment. But the UNDERLYING STRUCTURE was pure PUBLIC-CHOICE + RENT-SEEKING: a POLITICALLY CONNECTED DEVELOPER (concentrated beneficiary, capable of organizing) captured the STATE'S TAKINGS POWER to acquire property from DISPERSED HOMEOWNERS (concentrated cost per homeowner, dispersed across the neighborhood, unable to organize as effectively). The redevelopment justification (jobs, tax base) was the STATED PUBLIC PURPOSE; the ECONOMIC-BENEFICIARY analysis is the PUBLIC-CHOICE reading. The reasoning move for policy analysis: WHENEVER government coercion is deployed to transfer resources between private parties on 'public purpose' justification, examine WHO IS the concentrated beneficiary and WHO IS the concentrated cost-bearer. That analysis often reveals a rent-seeking structure the stated justification obscures.
